chapter: Melvin Moore, Hammond and the New York trip
title: The trumpet section and the slow reader Amos Woodruff
summary: Press calls Fields a cross between Duke and the Count; Amos Woodruff is a fine soloist but reads slowly, while Jeff Carrington and the Milton twins share first trumpet.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: So then I said I will wait and see when exactly we're going to leave and I'll let my man work on, because he's been very fair with me--Hobart--I said when I get some idea of when we would leave, I'll get you in time, a couple of weeks before we're going. So I began to get the trade magazines, this and that and
so on, a cross between the Duke and the Count, Ernie Fields that he discovered in there.
So everybody was smiling and everything and there was this Amos Woodruff who I just loved as a musician and everything but that was the only member in the band that read slow--
What did he play?
Trumpet.

A terrific soloist; when he played a solo he never did break the tone. It was just as beautiful as he was playing a sweet solo. If you knew anything about Harold Baker or Louie, that's the kind of style that he played, and he read so slow and you'd have to wait and drill and drill.
Who was first in the band?
Jeff Carrington, a young man out of San Antonio, Texas, out of Texas University--what was that black school, not the University of Texas--
Southern University?
Southern is in New Orleans, isn't it? I mean Louisiana.
You're talking about the one in Houston?
Yeah. Jeff hadn't finished college, but he was from there--
Texas Southern.
Yeah. We'd switch between he and Edwin Milton.
I had two brothers, I had twins in the band, Edwin Milton, a trumpet and Edward on trombone.
Edwin would be on first or either Jeff between and Amos would play second or third all the time.
So anyway--
Amos Woodruff?
Woodruff.
